Aggregate tiers with no recorded configuration will be disabled, and unrecorded external rules will be lost. Check with the database administrator before proceeding.

The GiB limit applies only to raw Historian samples and includes TimescaleDB chunks, indexes and auxiliary data. It does not limit aggregates, alarms, events, Audit, the primary database or server free space. Aggregates keep their own retention policy.

Under When the limit is reached, Warn only shows a warning without deleting data. Delete complete oldest chunks requires confirmation of permanent raw-sample loss. Every minute, maintenance can remove up to four complete old time intervals and keeps the newest interval. Chunk size makes this a target rather than an instant ceiling; usage may remain above it.

The size limit and retention by days can coexist; whichever condition removes samples first takes effect. Review the measurement after maintenance and plan with a margin. If samples must be kept outside the active database, configure and monitor archiving before a retention or size policy removes them.

Under Archive and restore samples, create an archive for a selected period or configure scheduled archiving. An archive contains raw Historian samples only. It does not include aggregates, alarms, events, Audit, the project, Authority, licensing, or HA state. Dates entered in the browser are converted to UTC.

In the schedule, Start archiving from sets the initial cursor. Archive only data at least this many days old leaves a buffer for recent data. Run every controls when the next batch may start; Archive up to per run limits the number of days handled in one batch. SCADIVO advances the cursor only after the archive is verified and completed. A blocked job needs the destination fixed and a manual resume; source data stays available.

Keep archive files without an expiry date to retain .scadhist packages. If you set a retention period, rotation removes completed archive files older than that many days; it does not remove database samples. In Docker, mount the destination folder on persistent storage. If the API has multiple nodes, all nodes must use the same shared persistent folder; different local folders cannot be a common archive destination.

Source removal is separate from file rotation and starts unchecked. It starts only after the complete package has been read back and verified. Progress is saved one segment at a time in the same transaction as that segment's source deletion; after a restart, already confirmed segments are skipped and later-arriving samples remain in the database. The batch is marked Completed only after every authorized segment is processed. The schedule requires its own confirmation. Check the cursor and job state, and test a restore before relying on archiving to free space. If the raw-sample size limit removes chunks before the cursor reaches them, those samples can no longer be archived.

To restore, choose a .scadhist file and select Verify and restore. SCADIVO validates the entire package before inserting samples. For each segment, it compares how many identical occurrences are already present and inserts only the missing rows, avoiding duplicates that remain in the database. Progress is recorded in the active Historian. Repeating the archive does not duplicate samples and can refill data removed later by a retention policy. Keep copies outside the rotated folder if you need the files longer.

sections.heading: Prepare the target
sections.body:
Ask the administrator for the destination details: server address, database, account, permissions and certificates. Make a backup and agree a maintenance window before migrating. Migration may pause writes.

The connection comes from the SCADIVO service. Opening an address in a browser therefore does not prove the service can reach it. In Docker, localhost means the container itself; use a name or address the service can actually access.

Likewise, the certificate file must exist on the server running the service, whether Windows, Linux or a container. A path available only on the browser computer does not meet that requirement.

sections.heading: Migrate data to another database
sections.body:
1. Check which database is active and have a backup available.
2. Fill the Remote destination and use Validate destination. Validation checks connection, authentication, TLS protection and compatibility; connection alone is not enough to permit switching.
3. Prepare migration and review the plan: source, destination and included data. Configuration becomes locked after preparation.
4. During the maintenance window, use Start migration. Durable writes may be paused during the operation.
5. Wait for copying and automatic verification. Read the result before proceeding.
6. Only after successful verification, use Activate Remote database and confirm the destination.
7. If restart is requested, restart or reopen the service as appropriate for the installation. Before resuming, check active database, health, project and revision.

sections.heading: Connecting an existing database is not migration
sections.body:
Use Connect existing database (without copying) only when the destination is already prepared with the same project and active revision required by the installation. This path does not copy or merge records. Use migration to take current database data to a new destination.

Read the confirmation before switching. If project or revision is incompatible, the operation is blocked. Do not empty or modify the database to bypass this check.

sections.heading: Rollback and return to local storage
sections.body:
If Recovery/Rollback required appears, the operation needs recovery or reversal. Read diagnostics and use Roll back operation when available.

Returning to Local Managed checks and reactivates the preserved local database; restart may be required. It does not automatically merge data written to Remote after the switch. The previous database is preserved, but this is not the same as restoring a backup. It does not delete Remote either.

After returning, check which data, project and revision are actually active before resuming operation.

sections.heading: Basic and advanced fields
sections.body: To prepare Remote, start with the address, username and password supplied by the administrator. Other fields can keep their filled values when suitable for the installation. Open Advanced settings to review or change those details. The table below explains each choice; examples are not real credentials.

fields.label: Host / FQDN
fields.description: Service-reachable PostgreSQL DNS name/address, not the web UI URL.

fields.label: User / identity
fields.description: PostgreSQL application account; not your SCADIVO Authority login.

fields.label: Password / secret
fields.description: Sent without being returned in status. Clearing after submission does not mean the credential was lost. Never paste into tickets or captures.
fields.example: Enter only in the protected form

fields.label: Database
fields.description: Target database name, not project name. Initial value is elitescada; confirm with the administrator.

fields.label: Port
fields.description: PostgreSQL port. Initial value 5432 differs from the application HTTPS port.

fields.label: TLS mode
fields.description: TLS protects the connection. Require demands encryption; VerifyCa also checks the certificate authority chain; VerifyFull additionally checks the server name. Prefer and Disable do not guarantee the same protection. Use the mode agreed with IT; do not disable TLS just to hide an error.
fields.example: Require or VerifyFull with valid CA

fields.label: CA certificate path
fields.description: CA file readable by the service; required by the form for VerifyCa/VerifyFull. A browser-computer path does not serve another host/container.

fields.label: Timeout (s)
fields.description: Connection wait; initially 15 seconds. Increasing it does not fix credentials, DNS or certificates.

fields.label: Historian uses Primary / dedicated
fields.description: When checked, recorded history, called Historian, uses the primary database. Clear only if you prepared a dedicated history database. Then fill its complete connection details and validate that destination’s compatibility too.
fields.example: Use Primary for a simple setup

sections.heading: Errors requiring different actions
sections.body:
Start with the message received. For no connection, check name/address, port and access from the service. Authentication refusal calls for checking the PostgreSQL account and password. A TLS error calls for checking the certificate authority, server name and certificate validity.

For incompatibility, read PostgreSQL version, TimescaleDB requirements when applicable and schema, the data structure the product expects. For invalid phase, refresh state and follow Next action; do not start another copy while one is in progress.

When the database is unavailable, Runtime can be degraded. The product must not present memory writes as database persistence. For support, record time, phase and operation ID; omit passwords.

en.title: HA: configure two servers and monitor operation
en.summary: Distinguish saved configuration, active server, ready partner and duplicate-execution protection.

sections.heading: What to prepare first
sections.body:
HA means High Availability. Two servers are prepared so Runtime can move between them with protection against duplicate execution. In this guide, node means either of those servers.

Open Engineering > High Availability. Observation requires the HA Runtime license and permission to monitor the servers. Saving or operating also requires transfer permission. Check service-to-service networking, authentication, clocks and storage on both nodes.

Databases may be shared or separate according to the prepared installation. Enabling HA does not create data replication or guarantee database availability. Check that part with the installation administrator before configuring the pair.

sections.heading: Enter only installation-dependent settings
sections.body: The screen calls the nodes This server and Partner server. Start with addresses that allow their services to communicate. Use the picker for preferred server and the protected authentication flow. The product handles internal identities and automatic transport; do not invent those values. The table details the choices.

fields.label: Each server main address
fields.description: Endpoint reachable by services. A browser-detected address is useful only if the partner reaches it too; localhost on two hosts is not one server.

fields.label: External address override
fields.description: Open only when the network requires a different advertised address. Otherwise keep automatic values to avoid inconsistent targets.
fields.example: No override on a simple network

fields.label: Preferred server
fields.description: Startup/failback preference; does not force promotion or establish readiness.

fields.label: Inter-server authentication
fields.description: Configure the shared secret through the protected flow on both nodes. Submitted values clear from the form; inspect authentication state without capturing the secret.

fields.label: Protection and shared reference
fields.description: This reference supports protection against two Active servers at once, called fencing. Both must see the same shared external storage. Two local files with matching names are not one common reference.
fields.example: Shared resource provisioned for the installation

fields.label: Automatic failover
fields.description: Allows eligible automatic takeover and requires protection. It does not replace partner readiness, available data or safety conditions.

sections.heading: Preparation procedure
sections.body:
1. Check Running mode before editing. It reports the configuration the service is using now.
2. Prepare HA, enter both service addresses and choose the preferred server.
3. Configure authentication and shared protection. Resolve items shown under HA readiness.
4. Use Save desired configuration. This stores the choice but does not prove it is already Running.
5. If restart is pending, plan it and then check the configuration actually loaded by the services.
6. Refresh state. Check effective Active, partner readiness, database and protection. Standby alone does not mean Ready Standby.
7. Before process use, perform the manual exercise agreed with the installation administrator. This guide’s checks do not replace that evaluation.

sections.heading: Read states before operating
sections.body:
Effective Active is the server authorized to execute now. It may not be the preferred one. The partner may merely be in Standby, waiting, or in Ready Standby, with readiness evaluated by the server. Read that distinction before transferring.

Synchronizing means synchronization is still in progress. Promoting and Demoting are transitions: wait for the result. Stale warns that the observation is old. Isolated, Faulted, degraded state or ambiguous authority call for diagnosis.

Check database availability separately from partner communication. Reaching the partner does not prove the database works. Increasing network tolerances to hide a database fault does not resolve it.

sections.heading: Choose the right operation
sections.body:
Choose the action for the situation. Switchover is a planned transfer from effective Active to an eligible partner. Failback requests return to the preferred server when allowed. Recovery reconciles a failure or blocked condition.

Force resynchronization has a specific condition: there must be no Active, and the previous authority must be fenced, meaning prevented from continuing execution. The action does not let the operator declare a partner ready.

Before confirming, read action and target. Afterwards check result, history and which node is Active. If the request is refused, investigate the cause before trying again.

sections.heading: Advanced settings: meaning and bounds
sections.body:
Initially keep the filled timing values. They control how long information is recent and how protection responds to failures.

Adjust only after assessing network, clocks and operation. A number fitting the form’s limit does not make it a recommendation for your installation. The table explains each timing’s effect.

For checking permissions in Security: HighAvailabilityObserve allows observation; HighAvailabilityTransfer is also required for saving and operating. These are reference identifiers for the administrator.

fields.label: Freshness (s)
fields.description: Maximum time for treating an observation as recent. After that it may be too old to guide operation; this is not a TAG acquisition interval.

fields.label: Lease (s)
fields.description: Lifetime of the temporary authorization for the server to execute as Active. Once expired, that authority is no longer valid. Lease is not a commercial license.

fields.label: Poll (ms)
fields.description: Time between checks of the shared reference. A lower value checks more often. This field uses milliseconds, not seconds.

fields.label: Maximum witness age (s)
fields.description: Maximum age of partner-ready evidence; does not create readiness.
fields.constraints: At least Lease; up to 600 s

fields.label: Clock margin (s)
fields.description: Allowance for clock difference; not a substitute for time synchronization.
fields.constraints: 0 to floor(Lease/3)

sections.heading: If there is a problem
sections.body:
For a 403 response, check permission to observe or operate. If Saved differs from Running, check for pending restart. For an unavailable partner, examine addresses, networking and authentication between services.

If the protection reference is unavailable, investigate shared external storage. If the partner is not ready, read synchronization, database and diagnostic information; do not force promotion to bypass the condition.

Investigate one problem at a time. Record time, action, result and effective server for support, without the authentication secret.

en.title: Intelligence: enable, pause and resolve blocks
en.summary: Choose which equipment to analyze, prepare its configuration and activate use. Having the license does not automatically start analyses.

sections.heading: Follow the full sequence
sections.body:
Start with one piece of equipment, such as Pump 01. Open Engineering > Asset Intelligence. You will gather its variables, identify which equipment they belong to and choose where to use analysis.

The profile lists signals and their meanings. An assignment connects that profile to registered Equipment. Configure contexts and stages only when they fit your question. Then save, publish and activate the project revision.

One separate decision remains: explicitly activate the selected resource to allow analyses. Creating the profile, checking a box or having the license does not do that for you.

sections.heading: Permissions and resource selection
sections.body:
Your account needs permission to edit Engineering and manage Intelligence for the selected equipment or locations. Security shows these as EngineeringModify and AssetProcessIntelligenceManage. The latter needs an explicit grant, global or scoped to the resource. A role name such as Developer or SystemAdmin does not by itself establish that grant.

Queries also require TrendUse and the Intelligence license. If a control is blocked, check the session’s effective capabilities there. Choose resources through the pickers; there is no need to memorize or invent IDs.

sections.heading: Activate only where useful
sections.body:
1. Under Eligible scopes, select only the equipment or locations you want to analyze. Here, scope means that selection of resources.
2. Save the scopes and prepared configuration.
3. Publish and activate the project revision. Resolve pending changes before allowing execution.
4. On the resource row, use Activate and check that its execution permit is armed, meaning execution is allowed for that resource.
5. Open the assignment query, choose a period and request analysis. Activation allows a query; it does not automatically run one.
6. Use Pause to stop analyses. Pending work is cancelled, while TAGs and history remain. Pause a resource before removing it from the selection.

sections.heading: Configured active does not mean armed
sections.body:
If a permission was revoked, a resource can remain marked Active in configuration while execution is blocked. These are different facts: what was configured and what is authorized now.

Restoring the grant does not silently restart work. Check status and use Activate again, including after restart when requested by the screen. This requires an explicit decision by the responsible person. Check this condition before investigating missing data in the recorded history, called Historian.

sections.heading: Example: start small
sections.body:
For Pump 01, start with current and speed if those measurements exist. Choose analyses that accept them. When more measurements become available, you can expand the profile and use other compatible analyses.

Keep unused resources paused. Do not invent a missing vibration signal. Selection limits what is allowed to run, but does not guarantee fixed processor or memory usage.

en.title: Intelligence: signal meaning and units
en.summary: Describe what was measured, not just the TAG name.

sections.heading: Why a name is not enough
sections.body:
Before calculating, specify what each variable measures. A TAG named Power might be active power, apparent power or a calculation; Pressure might measure suction, discharge or their difference. Its name alone does not identify the right formula.

In the profile, choose the required semantic role: the option that identifies the signal’s meaning for analysis. Then fill in its displayed qualifiers, the details that make that choice precise. Legacy role text remains a description; it does not replace this selection.

sections.heading: Fields and choices
sections.body: Use this table when a profile field is unclear. Pickers show options accepted by the current catalog. Choose what matches the instrument and process, even if another option would unlock a calculation.

fields.label: Required
fields.description: Marks signals whose absence compromises requested coverage. Do not mark essential signals optional just to obtain a result.

fields.label: Semantic role
fields.description: Choose what the signal represents in the calculation: its quantity and function in the machine. Analysis uses that controlled option; it does not guess from the TAG name.

fields.label: Current basis
fields.description: Specify the current basis supplied by the instrument and accepted by the role, such as RMS when appropriate. If its label only says current, confirm the measurement before choosing.

fields.label: Signal kind
fields.description: Distinguishes measurement, reference and the role-required function. A setpoint does not prove a measured value.

fields.label: Pressure reference
fields.description: Specify which pressure was measured. Outlet minus inlet pressure differs from discharge pressure alone; choose the basis required by the role and confirmed by the instrument.

fields.label: Flow direction
fields.description: Identifies transfer direction; the opposite direction may invalidate a rule.

fields.label: Frequency reference
fields.description: Identifies frequency meaning per catalog; distinguish electrical reference from physical speed.

fields.label: TAG and unit
fields.description: Select the actual TAG and check its controlled engineering unit. A profile label change does not convert data. Some calculations require specific catalog units/versions.
fields.example: kW for power when it matches actual data

sections.heading: Example: do not confuse a proxy with efficiency
sections.body:
Suppose pump current rises while speed stays the same. That can guide an investigation, but current alone does not calculate the motor’s physical efficiency. It is a substitute indicator, also called a proxy.

Other rules may use electrical input power, flow and pressure difference. They become available only when signals meet the required roles, units and alignment. If a measurement or necessary detail is missing, read the reason for unavailability; do not enter fictional values to unlock the rule.

en.title: Intelligence: query results and build dashboards
en.summary: Start by checking data for the period. Then choose a calculation and, if needed, generate a screen for Runtime queries.

sections.heading: Start with coverage
sections.body:
Coverage answers the first question: is there usable data for this analysis? With the assignment saved and execution authorized, open the profile’s coverage query. Choose start and end and request the query.

The form shows local times; the query also identifies its UTC window, the common time reference used to compare data. End must be after start.

Check which required signals have data, accepted and rejected sample counts, quality and time alignment. Only then interpret minimum, maximum or average. A large sample count alone does not prove gap-free data or that all signals were measured together.

sections.heading: Performance: choose an eligible rule
sections.body:
In Performance, choose the calculation rule from the catalog. If an option is disabled, read which signal, meaning or unit is missing. Choosing another quantity merely to obtain a number would change the question.

Fill From/To and query. Read status, unit, actual period and limitations alongside the result. Unavailable is not zero. A substitute indicator, such as a current comparison, must not be presented as physical efficiency.

If assignment, revision or parameters change, request another query. The previous result belongs to the previous choices.

sections.heading: Two context types with different bounds
sections.body:
Context describes an operating condition so similar situations can be compared. For example, studying a pump within a flow range can be more useful than mixing every condition. There are two different configurations:

In the saved operating profile, a numeric range includes both limits in the current engineering unit. Signals need evidence at the exact same source UTC timestamp. Readings merely close in time do not meet that requirement.

In the contextual-deviation screen generator, choose 2 to 8 target signals and two numeric context signals. Context signals must differ from each other and from the targets: at least four usable numeric signals are needed. Ranges use the displayed controlled unit and include the lower limit but exclude the upper: lower ≤ value < upper.

Check which configuration you are using before copying limits. Units and upper-limit inclusion can differ.

sections.heading: Generate the screen and check the full chain
sections.body:
1. Choose the equipment assignment or process stage and the desired screen type.
2. Complete the requested signals and options. If the button is blocked, read the reason beside the field.
3. Generate the draft. This organizes objects and references; it does not yet read Historian data or activate the screen.
4. In the editor, check title, dimensions, objects, bindings and how to open the screen. Run Preview and Apply to put the edit in the project.
5. Save the revision, publish and activate. Open the Runtime screen through configured navigation.
6. In the analysis object, set the period and request the query. Check window and result. A stage screen groups its equipment; that does not create an aggregate indicator or establish that one equipment caused another’s result.

sections.heading: How to investigate an empty result
sections.body:
If there is no result, look for the first missing condition:

Check license and permissions, then the resource’s saved selection and armed execution permit. Check that the active project and revision are the expected ones. Next review assignment, TAGs and period.

If those are correct, examine Historian capture, data quality, signal roles/units and alignment/context requirements. Correct the condition shown to be missing and query again.

Do not change a signal’s meaning or widen limits merely to produce a result. Analyses support investigation. They do not confirm defects or predict failures with field validity that has not yet been demonstrated.

en.title: Where to start in SCADIVO
en.summary: Choose what you need to do now. You do not need to configure every area before building your first screen.

sections.heading: If this is your first application
sections.body: Start with First project. It shows how to create a test variable, display its value and check the result. Complete that small exercise before adding alarms, reports or analysis. Then add the features your application needs.

sections.heading: Bring a reading into the system
sections.body: A TAG is a named variable, such as temperature or pump state. Data Sources selects where readings come from; TAGs specifies which reading to use. Before drawing a screen, check the value and its validity in TAG Monitor. First project uses a test variable so you can learn without equipment.

sections.heading: Build the operator screen
sections.body: Use Screens to place text, drawings and values. A Popup is a supporting window, such as pump details. When several pumps share a drawing, a Template helps reuse it. Learn those reuse options after building a simple first screen.

sections.heading: Store data and follow events
sections.body: To inspect yesterday’s values, configure Historian recording and query History or Trends. To warn about a condition such as high pressure, configure an alarm. Reports organize results for viewing/export. Intelligence helps analyze equipment and processes; it is not required to display a reading.

sections.heading: Prepare access and maintenance
sections.body: Security defines who can sign in and which actions they may perform. Licensing shows available installation features/limits. Database and high-availability pages support infrastructure setup. Visit them when the task requires it; you do not need to learn them all before the first exercise.

sections.heading: Find a field explanation
sections.body: Open Help from the page where the question arose. You can also search for a field or task, such as creating a screen. Read the procedure first. Use tables to look up a field and Technical reference only when you need its internal name. Related links suggest another subject; they are not compulsory reading.

en.title: Header and Mobile: presentation and navigation
en.summary: Configure visual identity and choose the right screen for a device.

sections.heading: The header is not the process screen
sections.body:
The header groups branding, titles, shortcuts and clock above the process screen. Configure it in Engineering > Header. It helps identify and navigate the application; editing it changes no TAGs and adds no objects to the screen drawing.

Use Validate preview and Apply to Working, the project draft. Then save, publish and activate the revision to use the change in Runtime.

fields.label: Brand presentation
fields.description: Default uses SCADIVO; Text uses entered text; Image uses a project asset; Hidden removes branding.

fields.label: Text and subtitle
fields.description: Title identifies the application; subtitle adds context. With an image the text also provides accessible identification.
fields.constraints: Text up to 128; subtitle up to 256 characters

fields.label: Project image
fields.description: Select/import a supported file. This is not a camera URL; use Media Sources for that.

fields.label: Height and colors
fields.description: Height occupies usable space. Follow theme retains theme colors; custom colors override that choice.
fields.example: Check readability on desktop and mobile
fields.constraints: Height 56–168 px

fields.label: Title, screen name and typography
fields.description: Select alignment and font/size/weight/color. Showing screen name follows navigation without renaming the screen.

fields.label: Control position and order
fields.description: Moves navigation as a group to the chosen side; order arranges relative position. User menu remains rightmost.

fields.label: Date and time
fields.description: Enable if useful; select mode, format, position and order. This clock is not TAG acquisition time.

fields.label: Screen shortcuts
fields.description: For each button choose label, existing screen and optional image. The screen must exist in the active revision.
fields.constraints: Up to 16 editor shortcuts

sections.heading: Mobile: orientation and variant
sections.body:
In Engineering > Mobile, choose presentation on touch devices. Orientation selects Landscape or Portrait; physical orientation lock depends on the browser.

For each desktop screen, use the same screen or select an existing alternative. Draw that alternative yourself in Screens: selecting Portrait does not automatically rearrange objects. Both use the same TAGs and Runtime without copying data. To change the application’s top area, return to Header.

sections.heading: Procedure and verification
sections.body: 1. Configure branding and necessary shortcuts. 2. Validate/apply. 3. Design a mobile variant in Screens and select it in Mobile if needed. 4. Validate/apply Mobile. 5. Save/publish/activate. 6. Check Runtime on desktop/mobile for buttons, navigation, readability and orientation. For an old layout inspect active revision; for a missing image inspect the selected asset.

en.title: Media Sources: camera, address and credential
en.summary: Register the source, then choose its visual presentation.

sections.heading: Source and object are separate steps
sections.body:
First prepare the video or image origin in Engineering > Media Sources. The source says where content comes from. Then select it in the Screen object, which defines where it appears and how it is presented.

RTSP needs the server relay, the service forwarding the stream for playback. Registering a source does not mean the browser plays RTSP directly. Check that infrastructure before changing multiple parameters to fix playback.

fields.label: Display name
fields.description: Identifies the camera/source in the list.

fields.label: Stable key
fields.description: Unique reference; use letters, numbers, dot, hyphen or underscore.

fields.label: Protocol
fields.description: Choose the source format: HTTP/HTTPS, HLS, MJPEG or RTSP/RTSPS. Changing this option does not convert content.
fields.example: HLS when the source provides HLS

fields.label: Address
fields.description: Absolute URL without username, password, query parameters or fragment. Credentials belong in the protected form.

fields.label: Enabled
fields.description: Controls source enablement in configuration; does not prove reachability or playback.

fields.label: Protected credentials
fields.description: After creating the source select Basic user/password or Bearer token. Save separately. They are write-only and excluded from packages; configure again on the target host.
fields.example: Use the protected panel, not a password URL

sections.heading: Procedure and common problems
sections.body:
1. Create the source with name, key, protocol, address and enabled state.
2. Save it. If credentials are needed, configure them in the created source’s panel.
3. Insert or select a compatible visual object and choose the supported source.
4. Save, publish and activate; check playback in Runtime.

For no playback, check address/protocol, service-side access, host credentials, relay when required and active revision. Removing credentials can prevent camera access. Project export does not carry its password.

en.title: Home/Building: locations and devices
en.summary: Organize device locations and inspect their actual capabilities.

sections.heading: Separate location, device and connection
sections.body:
In Engineering > Home/Building, first organize where a device is. Location may be a room or area. Equipment is the device instance, such as a light. Data Source stores the connection used to communicate.

These are different facts: moving a light to another room does not change its protocol. Start with devices and TAGs the connection actually offers.

fields.label: Location name
fields.description: Readable name within the hierarchy.

fields.label: Location kind
fields.description: Choose Site, Building, Floor, Area/Room or Zone. The kind grants no permissions and creates no automation.

fields.label: Parent location
fields.description: Where it belongs. Choose an existing parent and avoid circular relationships; no parent represents a root where allowed.

fields.label: Device location
fields.description: Assigns an instance to an existing Location; organizes the project rather than testing communication.

fields.label: Device name and path
fields.description: Name is a label; path is a stable reference. Review the candidate before applying and preserve identity when reorganizing.
fields.example: Check instance and reference in preview

sections.heading: Procedure and verification
sections.body: 1. Configure connectivity and inspect supplied TAGs/capabilities. 2. Create location hierarchy with name, kind and parent. 3. Assign devices to locations and review identity. 4. Preview and apply only the validated candidate. 5. Save/publish/activate. 6. Test readings/actions in a test installation. Displaying equipment does not create missing capabilities/commands; inspect provider, mapping and permissions. For graphical faceplates see Equipment and Templates.

en.title: Reports: configure data, period and resolution
en.summary: Start with the question the report should answer before drawing the page.

sections.heading: Prepare verifiable data
sections.body:
Start with the question: which readings should appear, and for what period? In Engineering > Reports, first use a pressure TAG with existing history and a short interval with known values. This lets you check data before designing the page.

The report queries stored records. It does not enable capture or recover an unrecorded past. Your account needs permission to edit and query the chosen source. Use the samples dataset for values and the alarm dataset for alarm transitions.

sections.heading: First test before final layout
sections.body:
1. Choose an embedded query, which belongs to the report, and historian.samples, the samples dataset.
2. Add a known TAG through the reference picker.
3. Choose a short period and Raw resolution.
4. Run Preview. Check available rows, times, values and quality.
5. Switch to Summary with Maximum and an hourly interval. Compare each output with raw data: an interval maximum is not a list of every reading.
6. Then arrange the page and validate the definition. For no preview rows, check TAG, period, capture and permission before changing colors or widths.

sections.heading: Identification and query source
sections.body: Create or select a report. Use reference selectors instead of inventing IDs. These fields configure the definition; executing a preview is separate.

fields.label: Name, identifier and description
fields.description: Name appears in the list; identifier preserves references; description explains purpose/context. Renaming creates no new data.

fields.label: Saved Data Query or embedded query
fields.description: A Data Query reuses an existing definition; an embedded query belongs to the report. Check the selection before changing layout. The editor does not accept arbitrary SQL.
fields.example: Embedded query for the first example

fields.label: Data source / dataset
fields.description: historian.samples queries samples; alarm.events queries alarm occurrences/transitions. Fields depend on this choice; switching datasets may invalidate layout fields.

fields.label: Default period and preview period
fields.description: Default belongs to the definition; preview period selects the current test window. Use the editor unit. One hour is 3600 seconds; this is not a row count.
fields.example: Last hour to check a small sample

fields.label: Report data / variables
fields.description: Add TAGs through the reference browser. Check path, type and unit; configure each variable presentation separately.

fields.label: Rows per page
fields.description: Requested query page size; inspect the returned count. It does not define Historian retention duration.

sections.heading: Choose data retrieval/presentation
sections.body:
Resolution defines how to retrieve and summarize records for this query. Raw shows stored samples; other options organize or summarize output. Check raw values before using a summary.

This choice does not change captured data, remove raw records or configure permanent database aggregation policy.

fields.label: Raw, fixed interval or summary
fields.description: Raw examines stored samples; fixed interval retrieves on defined steps; summary applies a function per bucket. An average may hide a peak; inspect raw data to investigate.
fields.example: Raw for checking; hourly summary for overview

fields.label: Fixed interval
fields.description: Choose spacing between retrieval positions. It is neither Driver polling nor a guarantee of a sample at every position. Missing data remains significant.
fields.example: 5 minutes if suitable for the question

fields.label: Aggregation and bucket
fields.description: Average, min, max, sum, count, first and last differ. Choose bucket width. Summing flow readings does not automatically calculate production volume; integration and appropriate units would be needed.
fields.example: Hourly maximum to look for peaks

fields.label: Long or wide table
fields.description: Long organizes sample rows; wide organizes intervals for comparing variables. Wide is disabled for raw mode.

en.title: Reports: page, variables, fields and summaries
en.summary: Separate the queried value, its format and where it is printed.

sections.heading: Understand the page
sections.body:
In the Designer, Project/Design is where you build the page; Preview shows a run with data. Start with a title and one reading field before adding groups and totals.

Dimensions use millimeters, as on a printed page, not Runtime-screen pixels. Portrait is vertical; Landscape is horizontal. Reserve margins and fit content in the remaining width. Zoom only changes how you see Preview, not print size.

sections.heading: How to format a variable
sections.body: The variable remains linked to its selected TAG. These fields change presentation, not calibration or conversion by relabelling.

fields.label: Show column and order
fields.description: Choose visibility and use Move up/down for order. Removing a report variable does not delete its TAG.

fields.label: Display label
fields.description: Readable variable heading, distinct from TAG identity.

fields.label: Automatic, hidden or custom unit label
fields.description: Automatic uses the TAG unit; Hidden omits it; custom label changes text only. Labelling a bar value psi does not convert it.
fields.example: Automatic when the unit is correct

fields.label: Decimals and numeric format
fields.description: Choose standard, fixed or scientific. Decimals affect display, not accuracy or stored value. Do not round away relevant variation.
fields.constraints: 0–15 places in the editor

fields.label: Date/time and Boolean labels
fields.description: Choose local date/time, date, time or ISO 8601. Set meaningful True/False labels; missing data is not False.
fields.example: Running / Stopped only if that is the meaning

sections.heading: Layout sections and controls
sections.body:
Label is fixed text, such as Discharge pressure. Field shows a query value. These are the controls directly offered for insertion; start with them.

Put the title in the report header and record fields in Detail, the section receiving query rows. Page header/footer repeat on each page; report header/footer belong to the report. Group headers/footers depend on configured grouping.

With no query rows, a title can appear while Detail stays empty. Check data first rather than trying to fix this by increasing section height.

fields.label: Section height
fields.description: Reserved band space. A taller control can be clipped; increasing height creates no data rows.
fields.example: Fit the band to its content

fields.label: X, Y, width and height (mm)
fields.description: Layout position/size. Check section bounds and usable width; these are not monitor coordinates.

fields.label: Label text
fields.description: Fixed content such as a title. Use Field for row values; typing a TAG path into a label creates no binding.

fields.label: Query and field
fields.description: Query selects a result; Field must exist in its dataset. Use its exposed schema name, such as value or timestamp for samples, not an invented name.

fields.label: Image asset
fields.description: An image control needs an existing resolved asset. If the picker does not offer it, do not invent an ID; use editable controls and check configuration availability.

sections.heading: Grouping is not temporal aggregation
sections.body:
Group by brings rows together by the chosen field and lets you order that organization. Resolution defines query time intervals. These are different choices: naming a group does not change the interval.

For a summary, choose field, function and scope: just the group or the whole report. Check whether the query already summarized data before summing again. Count reports record quantity, not running hours. Test a small group and check its total manually.

sections.heading: From preview to active revision
sections.body:
1. Build a title, Detail section and fields linked to real data.
2. Run Preview and check data, pages and clipping.
3. Use Validate and correct invalid references or structure.
4. Apply only the valid candidate. If the project changed during editing, refresh and validate again.
5. Save, publish and activate the revision through project controls.
6. Generate the report in Runtime with the same test parameters and compare. Preview shows a run; it does not save the definition or prove the new revision is active.

en.title: Runtime reports: generate, check and export
en.summary: Output belongs to one execution with its own period and parameters.

sections.heading: Find the available report
sections.body:
Open Reports in Runtime and search by name. The list uses the active revision and your session’s permissions. If a report is missing, check those two conditions before recreating it.

Engineering access or seeing a report object on a screen does not grant access to every dataset. The generating user also needs permission to query the chosen source.

sections.heading: Period, parameters and execution
sections.body:
1. Select the report to generate.
2. Choose relative period or From/To from allowed modes. Relative is calculated at execution time: repeating later can use a different window.
3. For an absolute interval, enter start before end and check the displayed time zone.
4. Complete parameters with the requested types and options. Numbers, dates and booleans do not accept arbitrary text.
5. Use Generate report and wait. Cancel interrupts the request; it does not delete the definition.
6. Before interpreting, check generation time, queried period and parameters used.

sections.heading: Preview, PDF, spreadsheet and print
sections.body:
Check output with previous/next page and zoom. Fit to width changes only the view. Use PDF or print for paginated presentation; XLSX and CSV let you work with output data.

These export the result, not project-import packages or TAG edits. An exported file represents that run. Generate again to update data; reopening the file does not make a live query.

Before sharing a spreadsheet or CSV, check units, dates and decimal formatting expected by the recipient.

sections.heading: Problems needing different checks
sections.body:
For a missing report, review publication/activation and authorization. For a title with no rows, check period, filters and capture. For an empty field or error, confirm referenced field/query, type and parameters.

An unexpected number calls for checking resolution, function, unit and summary scope. A different label does not convert units. For clipping, check millimeters, usable width and section height.

If data looks old, check generation time and generate again. Do not change permissions or units blindly to try to fix output.

en.title: Historian: configure capture and check history
en.summary: Choose what to record, under which conditions and how to verify storage.

sections.heading: Where to configure and query
sections.body:
To see what happened earlier, SCADIVO must have recorded the data. Historian is that history of TAG samples. The live monitor shows the current value; History, Reports and Intelligence use what was stored. Enabling today does not recover an unrecorded past.

In Engineering > Historian, review TAGs with capture enabled and their summary. To change how a TAG records, open Engineering > TAGs, select it and expand History/Historian in the editor.

sections.heading: Example showing deadband effects
sections.body:
Deadband is the minimum change used to decide whether a new numeric observation should be recorded. It is compared with the last accepted value.

With constant quality, deadband 0.1 and last accepted value 1.00, observation 1.03 may be discarded. Value 1.12 exceeds the threshold and may be accepted. The next comparison starts from the last accepted value, not every discarded observation.

The first observation and quality changes have their own handling and may be recorded without that change. With a maximum-interval strategy, an observation received after the deadline may also be accepted. Do not calculate expected record count from deadband alone.

sections.heading: Verification procedure
sections.body:
1. Check the live TAG: value, type, scale and quality.
2. In the TAG editor, enable History and choose a strategy with valid required fields.
3. Run Preview and Apply; save, publish and activate the revision. Editing the draft alone does not change running capture.
4. On a test source, produce known changes and note when they occurred.
5. Open Runtime History, choose Samples and filter the TAG for that same period.
6. Compare values, quality, times and count against the configured strategy.
7. Repeat with a stable signal and a quality change. For Intelligence, also check source timestamp and the analysis’s alignment requirement.

sections.heading: TAG capture fields
sections.body: Use the accepted names below in the current strategy field. Unknown text or incomplete settings may retain legacy all-observation capture rather than expected volume reduction. Inspect configuration/samples instead of assuming savings from filling a field.

fields.label: History enabled
fields.description: Enables this TAG capture. Disabling neither deletes existing history nor creates a backup.
fields.example: Enable the pressure TAG used in the test

fields.label: Strategy
fields.description: periodic captures observations respecting a period; onChange records value changes; onChangeDeadband requires numeric variation; onChangeDeadbandMaxInterval adds a maximum interval between accepted arriving observations.

fields.label: Deadband
fields.description: Minimum absolute change from the last accepted captured value. It is neither a percentage nor alarm limit. Use a compatible numeric strategy.
fields.constraints: Finite number ≥ 0

fields.label: Period (ms)
fields.description: Used by periodic. 1000 ms = 1 second. It selects arriving observations, not faster Driver polling or invented samples when the source is silent.
fields.constraints: Positive integer

fields.label: Maximum period (ms)
fields.description: Used by onChangeDeadbandMaxInterval to accept an arriving observation when time elapses despite small change. Does not guarantee capture during communication outage.
fields.example: 60000 for up to one minute between accepts while observations arrive
fields.constraints: Positive integer

sections.heading: Query: period, filters and pages
sections.body:
Start by choosing the record collection, called a dataset. Value samples and alarm transitions are different collections. Select a short relative period or fill From/To; the current window allows up to 31 days per query.

Then use filters offered for that dataset. Each field expects a value type: number, boolean, date, text or enum. Choose an available operator and enter the right type rather than arbitrary text.

Sorting changes presentation order, not record selection. Moving pages continues the query; it does not extend its period. For no result, remove one filter at a time and check that capture existed at that time.

sections.heading: Capture, retention, backup and Playback differ
sections.body:
These are different decisions. Capture selects observations to record. Retention defines how long to keep them. Aggregation summarizes samples; backup keeps a recoverable copy. Configuring TAG capture does not define a global database quota or archiving.

Playback displays historical values. It does not restore the process or allow commands from the past. Return to live mode before operating. Missing samples do not mean zero or stopped equipment.

en.title: Alarms: configure condition, priority and behavior
en.summary: Configure a notice for a known condition and test what the operator will see. The example uses high pressure without commanding equipment.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body:
Start with one simple condition: notify when pressure reaches its high limit. In Engineering > Alarms, use a test TAG whose value, type, scale and unit you have checked. A TAG is the variable providing the reading.

The alarm observes that variable; it does not configure the sensor or stop the pump by itself. Agree the limit and operating response with the process owner. For learning, use simulation with the applicable Engineering permission and lock, without acting on real equipment.

sections.heading: Choosing a type
sections.body:
Choose the type by the question the alarm must answer:

Digital follows a boolean: choose whether true or false means an alarm condition. High and HighHigh activate when the value is greater than or equal to the limit (≥). Low and LowLow activate when less than or equal (≤). For two limits, create two definitions and choose each priority separately.

Communication follows reading quality: it activates when quality differs from Good and returns with Good. It uses no setpoint, the numeric limit, and selecting it alone creates no communication-loss timer. With poor quality, process alarms do not treat the number as a valid reading; use Communication to follow that condition.

System appears in the picker but has no generic process rule in this evaluator. For a high limit or boolean state, choose its own type rather than System as a substitute.

sections.heading: Procedure: test a high threshold
sections.body:
Here, 10 bar is only a teaching value. ACK means acknowledgement: the operator confirms awareness of the notice.

1. Create a high alarm for the simulated pressure TAG, with setpoint 10. Check the TAG’s bar unit.
2. Fill priority, area and a clear message. Keep Requires acknowledgement checked for this test.
3. Run Preview, read errors and apply to Workspace, the editing draft. If you edit again, validate again.
4. Save, publish and activate the correct revision. Applying to Workspace does not activate Runtime by itself.
5. With Good quality, send 9: the condition is Normal. Send 10: it becomes Active. Equality also activates.
6. Acknowledge in Runtime while keeping the TAG at 10: it becomes Acknowledged, but pressure has not changed. Send 9: it becomes Returned and leaves the active list because it already had ACK.
7. Activate again with 10 and return to 9 without acknowledging: Returned remains pending. Acknowledge and check that it leaves the active list. Query history for previous transitions.

sections.heading: Identity and condition
sections.body: Select New alarm or an existing definition. The path identifies the signal to evaluate; the name and message help operators understand the problem.

fields.label: Name
fields.description: Use a readable description distinguishing equipment and condition. Renaming does not change the observed TAG.

fields.label: TAG path
fields.description: Enter an existing TAG path. Check its already-scaled value in TAG Monitor before choosing the threshold.
fields.constraints: Not a Driver address or screen name.

fields.label: Type
fields.description: Chooses the comparison rule; consult the type explanation in this article. HighHigh is another limit definition, not an automatic priority.

fields.label: Setpoint (threshold)
fields.description: Shown for analog types. Enter a number in the current TAG unit. High/HighHigh activate at value ≥ threshold; Low/LowLow at value ≤ threshold.
fields.constraints: Equality also activates. This editor has no hysteresis field.

fields.label: Active digital value
fields.description: Only shown for Digital. Checked means true is the alarm condition; unchecked means false. Verify actual signal polarity.

fields.label: Priority
fields.description: Orders and highlights attention: low, medium, high or critical. Does not change the threshold, permission or shutdown logic.

fields.label: Class
fields.description: Classification label for organizing definitions. Typing a name does not install a protection rule.

fields.label: Area
fields.description: Process context also used for area-scoped action authorization. Use the name expected by the policy; entering an area grants no access.

fields.label: Message
fields.description: Explain the condition and location usefully for the operator. A written instruction does not execute a command.

sections.heading: Behavior and sound
sections.body: Expand Alarm behavior. Some options are saved in the definition but have current Runtime limitations, described alongside the field.

fields.label: Enabled
fields.description: Includes the definition in evaluation when the revision is activated. Disabling fixes neither the signal nor the physical cause.

fields.label: Activation delay (ms)
fields.description: Represents the intended delay. Current limitation: the value is saved but does not delay Runtime activation. Do not rely on it to filter chatter.
fields.constraints: Integer field; delay not yet applied.

fields.label: Requires acknowledgement
fields.description: Expresses the intent to require operator ACK. Current limitation: clearing it does not remove pending acknowledgement in Runtime, including after return.

fields.label: Allow shelving
fields.description: Allows this definition to enter a suppressed state through an available operation. The action still requires AlarmShelve permission. The Alarm Center described here has no shelving button.
fields.constraints: Not Mute sounds; no automatic expiry is promised.

fields.label: Sound profile / preview
fields.description: Choose none, short pulse, double, triple, rising or alternating and try the preview. In Runtime, operators must enable sounds in the browser. Volume, output device and browser permission affect playback.
fields.constraints: Muting in the browser does not acknowledge the alarm.

sections.heading: If the result differs
sections.body: Check the TAG/active revision, scaling/unit, boolean polarity, enablement and quality. High priority does not force activation. A chattering threshold gains no hysteresis from a different message or class. Preview validates a candidate; it does not prove field acquisition. Delay and ACK exemption retain the limitations described. If the project changes while editing, reload and validate again rather than applying an old candidate.

en.title: Runtime alarms: states, acknowledgement and sounds
en.summary: Read the current condition, acknowledge it and distinguish silence, return and history.

sections.heading: Where to look and how to interpret
sections.body:
Runtime Alarm Center helps identify what needs attention now. It shows the active list allowed for your session, counts and selected-row details. It is not the history of everything that happened.

Select a row and check equipment, message, priority, area, value and times. Details also show who acknowledged and when. IDs identify the exact definition for lookup or support; acknowledging does not require inventing or typing an ID.

sections.heading: States shown in details
sections.body:
ACK confirms that the operator is aware of the alarm. It is separate from the physical condition, so an acknowledged alarm can still be active.

The active list includes Active, Acknowledged and Returned still without ACK. It can become empty after items return and are acknowledged, while previous transitions remain in history. The table explains the states shown in details.

fields.label: Normal
fields.description: Condition is not active now; a previous cycle may exist in history.

fields.label: Active
fields.description: Condition is present and this cycle is not yet acknowledged.

fields.label: Acknowledged
fields.description: ACK recorded but the condition remains present. It does not mean the cause was resolved.

fields.label: Returned
fields.description: Condition is no longer active. Without ACK it remains pending in the active list. After ACK it leaves that list.

fields.label: Disabled
fields.description: Definition disabled for evaluation. Does not indicate healthy equipment.

fields.label: Shelved
fields.description: Notification suppressed by shelving. Value and underlying state continue to be tracked; removing suppression restores the current underlying state.
fields.constraints: The current center provides no button for this action.

sections.heading: Procedure: acknowledge a notification
sections.body:
1. Select the row. Read condition, value and time and confirm the equipment.
2. Follow the plant’s operating response for that condition.
3. Use Acknowledge alarm if your session permits it for that area. The technical permission is AlarmAcknowledge; a View Only session still cannot perform it.
4. Wait for confirmation and list refresh. If the server accepted ACK but rereading failed, refresh to check before repeating actions.
5. If the condition remains, the acknowledged alarm stays visible. If it has returned, it leaves the active list after ACK. A new activation creates another acknowledgement pending.

sections.heading: Sounds, mute and unavailability
sections.body:
To hear notices, use Enable alarm sounds in this browser session. Check support, volume and audio output. Profiles repeat while an alarm is pending, including Returned without ACK.

Muting is local: it does not acknowledge, disable or shelve. Shelving suppresses the notification. Acknowledging does not send a process command either. These are different effects.

For denied access, check login, session class and area permission. For missing data or unavailable service, refresh and consult Runtime diagnostics; changing a TAG does not resolve an authorization refusal. For past records, open History and choose alarm.events for the period. This dataset concerns alarms; operational.events and Audit serve other purposes.

en.title: Operational events: define, emit and query
en.summary: Record a process occurrence with context, distinguishing definitions, occurrences, alarms and Audit.

sections.heading: Choose the right resource
sections.body:
Use an operational event to record a fact, such as batch start or a mode change. Each emission creates an occurrence with its own time and identity. It maintains no active condition and requests no ACK.

Choose an alarm to follow a condition that activates and returns. Audit tracks security or administration actions and outcomes. A screen click is also called an event, but does not become an operational occurrence by itself.

First register the fact’s definition, then configure what emits it. Registration does not automatically emit. Associating a TAG only provides context; it creates no change trigger.

sections.heading: Procedure: prepare the definition and producer
sections.body:
1. Create the definition with required fields and a name/key distinguishing the fact. Add useful context.
2. Run Preview and fix duplicate keys or invalid references reported in diagnostics.
3. Apply to Workspace, then save, publish and activate the revision through project controls.
4. Prepare what will emit the occurrence. A Server Script can call emit_operational_event. Obtain the saved definition’s stable ID from project references or exported data; do not substitute its textual identifier.
5. Associate the handler, the Python function, with the appropriate Server trigger. Avoid Timer for a single transition: each call creates another occurrence, even with the same message.
6. Activate the revision containing the definition and Script.
7. Produce one controlled test fact and query operational.events in History, including execution time in the period.

sections.heading: Python example: one occurrence at initialization
sections.body:
This example records simulation initialization, not a pump’s physical start. The illustrative UUID is a definition ID: replace it with your saved definition’s stable ID.

In the Script editor, choose Server and associate Initialize with handler initialize. Writing the function does not create that association. It runs at each Script initialization; event carries trigger context and may be unused.

emit_operational_event(definition_id, message=None, context=None) returns None, not the occurrence ID. In the context dictionary, keys and values are text. Use str(value) to turn a calculated number into text before including it.

sections.heading: Definition fields
sections.body: Open Engineering > Operational Events and select New Operational Event. Define meaning and source first; expand Optional context when needed. Type/category/source labels are text from your convention, not connection settings.

fields.label: Display name
fields.description: Readable name for people.
fields.constraints: Up to 240 characters.

fields.label: Key
fields.description: Text key unique across definitions, case insensitive. Not the stable ID used by the Python API.
fields.constraints: Required; up to 160 characters.

fields.label: Type
fields.description: Describes the nature of the fact; does not select an alarm type.
fields.constraints: Required; up to 120 characters.

fields.label: Category
fields.description: Groups occurrences using your convention for search and analysis.
fields.constraints: Required; up to 120 characters.

fields.label: Source
fields.description: Semantically identifies what produces the fact. Entering server-script does not automatically create or bind a script.
fields.constraints: Required; up to 240 characters.

fields.label: Enabled
fields.description: Controls definition availability in the Runtime revision. Does not remove historical occurrences.

fields.label: Default message
fields.description: Text used if emission supplies no other message. An emission message may override it.
fields.constraints: Up to 4000 characters.

fields.label: Area (optional)
fields.description: Places the fact within the process organization; grants no user permission.
fields.constraints: Up to 240 characters.

fields.label: Equipment path (optional)
fields.description: Equipment context reference. Does not create equipment or a drawing.
fields.constraints: Up to 500 characters.

fields.label: TAG (optional)
fields.description: Choose an existing TAG; the editor stores its identity and path. No TAG is valid for a general fact.
fields.constraints: Association does not automatically monitor changes.

sections.heading: Query and troubleshoot
sections.body:
In History, choose operational.events, the operational-occurrence dataset. Adjust start/end and filters and check time, source, message and context. alarm.events contains alarm transitions; Audit records a different kind of action.

Extra context does not change definition type, category, source or identity, even with keys using those names. Up to 128 pairs are allowed, with keys up to 160 characters and values up to 4000; messages also have a 4000 limit. Include no passwords or secrets.

For a missing occurrence, check active revision, enabled definition, ID, handler connection, Script diagnostics, period and permission. Registering the definition alone produces no records. Emission failure does not authorize another route: emission must respect Runtime’s active authority.

en.title: Local users: create, assign roles and maintain access
en.summary: Register who signs in and distinguish account, role, session and license.

sections.heading: Before administering accounts
sections.body:
Open Engineering > Security to register who signs into this installation. Local accounts, passwords and permissions belong to Security Authority, the installation’s security store. They are not project objects or part of the engineering package. A local account is also different from a commercial portal account.

Managing users requires UserRoleAdmin or SystemAdmin. Editing the project does not grant that access. Before changing roles or passwords, check your current account and preserve at least one enabled local administrator.

sections.heading: Local session duration
sections.body: In Security, set when the product should ask the user to sign in again. The timer starts at login and sets the maximum lifetime of a local login; it is not an inactivity timer. Closing the browser does not end the session. The new duration applies to future logins, while open sessions keep the expiry they already received. Choose 5 to 1,440 minutes (5 minutes to 24 hours); the product's initial value is 480 minutes, or 8 hours, unless the installation defines a different initial value in server configuration.

sections.heading: Procedure: create and test an operator
sections.body:
1. Check available roles, which actions each allows and for which resources. If a suitable role is missing, prepare and apply policy first.
2. Use New user and fill login, name, private password and enabled state.
3. Select only needed roles and create the account.
4. For later edits, review the summary and confirm saving. Changing a field does not save by itself.
5. In another session, sign in with the new account and test one allowed reading and one action that must be denied. License and View Only/Interactive class still limit actions.
6. Return to the administrator account to correct grants if needed. One session does not prove access for two different users.

sections.heading: Account fields
sections.body: Use New user to create an identity. For an existing account, select it in the list; its login name is shown for identification and is not renamed by this form. Password is entered during creation or in the separate reset form, without exposing the current password.

fields.label: Username / login
fields.description: Name used to sign in. Do not confuse it with the readable display name.
fields.constraints: 3–200 characters; unique username.

fields.label: Display name
fields.description: Identifies the person readably. Changing it changes neither login nor roles.
fields.constraints: 1–300 characters.

fields.label: Password / New password
fields.description: Create an individual password and follow the policy accepted by the server. Reset replaces the password rather than recovering the previous one. Never copy passwords into messages, scripts or packages.
fields.constraints: The form requires at least 8 characters; the server validates the policy.

fields.label: Enabled
fields.description: Allows account use. Disabling deletes neither identity nor action history. Changes can invalidate the session; keep another administrative account available.

fields.label: Roles
fields.description: Select existing roles whose permissions match the work. Grants from assigned roles combine; adding a role removes no permission from another. Naming a role developer or administrator creates no privilege by itself.
fields.constraints: Check the grants, not just the name.

sections.heading: Reset, search and common problems
sections.body: Search filters name/login/role, and status separates enabled and disabled accounts; hiding a row does not disable an account. To reset a password, select the account, enter New password, review the impact and confirm. Account/role or password changes can end sessions; sign in again when requested. The system rejects removing the last enabled local administrative access and assigning nonexistent roles. A 401 calls for signing in again; 403 indicates insufficient permission. A project revision does not carry users, and importing .escadapkg does not restore Authority.

en.title: Roles and scopes: grant the action on the right resource
en.summary: Build explicit grants, check their reach and apply the validated Authority policy.

sections.heading: Account, role, capability and scope
sections.body:
Start with who can do what and where. The account identifies the person. A role gathers permissions assigned to an account. Each grant connects an allowed action to all resources or a specific scope. The interface calls the action a capability and its reach a scope.

Open Engineering > Security and the roles/capabilities/scopes panel. Policy belongs to the installation’s Authority, not the drawing or project package. A role name alone grants no access.

Viewing requires UserRoleAdmin. Validating/applying requires EngineeringModify together with UserRoleAdmin or SystemAdmin. Check these permissions before editing policy.

sections.heading: Procedure: prepare and apply a policy
sections.body:
1. Load current policy and check who will keep administering the installation.
2. Create a role or select one. Before changing it, check which users already receive it.
3. Add a grant for each needed action. Choose global or the correct hierarchy node. If including descendants, check which resources become covered.
4. For Intelligence, explicitly add AssetProcessIntelligenceManage: global or Equipment/Location with a valid resource link. SystemAdmin alone does not replace that grant when configuring tools.
5. Run policy Preview, correct errors and apply only the validated candidate. A new edit invalidates the previous preview.
6. Assign the role and test allowed/denied access with that account.
7. If another administrator changed policy, reload and redo against the current version. Do not force an old version or delete users to bypass conflict.

sections.heading: Role and grant fields
sections.body: New role creates a draft. Duplicate copies settings into another role, not users. In the displayed hierarchy, IDs identify existing nodes/resources; this panel lets you select nodes but provides no form for creating or rearranging the hierarchy. Do not invent a UUID to replace a missing node.

fields.label: Stable identifier
fields.description: Key used in user assignments. Edit before first Apply. It is protected afterward; changing Display name does not change the key.

fields.label: Display name
fields.description: Readable label for selecting and recognizing the role. Not its permission list.

fields.label: Description
fields.description: Explain purpose and intended reach to prevent later mistakes.
fields.example: Read the station and acknowledge its alarms

fields.label: Capability
fields.description: Select the specific action. Use the reference below; similar names do not make capabilities interchangeable.

fields.label: Scope
fields.description: Unscoped grants this capability globally. Selecting a node restricts that grant to the corresponding resource. Global does not mean all capabilities.

fields.label: Include descendants
fields.description: With a selected node, includes its descendants in the authorization hierarchy. Unchecked covers only that node. It is not a name/path prefix search.
fields.constraints: Disabled without a node.

sections.heading: Available action reference
sections.body: These are the options shown in the current version. Permission creates no resource, changes no license and bypasses no active revision, readiness, context or operation limit.

fields.label: View
fields.description: View Runtime; grants no commands.

fields.label: TagRead
fields.description: Read TAGs for the authorized resource/scope.

fields.label: CommandExecute
fields.description: Execute registered commands. Distinct from writing a process value.

fields.label: ProcessValueWrite
fields.description: Request a process-value write, such as a setpoint. Does not replace command permission.

fields.label: AlarmAcknowledge
fields.description: Acknowledge alarms; does not fix the physical cause.

fields.label: AlarmShelve
fields.description: Shelve/unshelve alarms through an available operation, subject to the definition.

fields.label: TrendUse
fields.description: Use authorized queries/trends.

fields.label: TrendSave
fields.description: Save trend settings where available; grants no general project editing.

fields.label: EngineeringView
fields.description: Read authorized Engineering.

fields.label: EngineeringModify
fields.description: Modify Engineering subject to Engineering Lock and operation-specific requirements.

fields.label: UserRoleAdmin
fields.description: Administer users/roles through authorized flows. Policy mutation also requires Engineering editing.

fields.label: SystemAdmin
fields.description: Administer system operations requiring this capability, such as querying Audit. Do not assume it replaces every specific capability.

fields.label: HighAvailabilityObserve
fields.description: Observe HA status.

fields.label: HighAvailabilityTransfer
fields.description: Request HA authority transfer subject to readiness and permissions.

fields.label: HighAvailabilityAdmin
fields.description: Administer HA settings. An operation may require other Engineering permissions.

fields.label: AssetProcessIntelligenceManage
fields.description: Manage Intelligence with an explicit global grant or a valid Equipment/Location restriction. License and activation remain necessary.

sections.heading: Preview, session and rejection
sections.body:
The selected account’s preview shows what roles in the draft appear to grant. It helps review the edit but does not decide access for a concrete resource. Displayed effective capabilities belong to your current session, not the selected person.

The server makes the final decision using person, resource and scope. Runtime also considers session class and license. Policy has its own Authority version and Preview/Apply; exporting or activating a project does not replace it.

The product refuses deletion of an assigned role or loss of the last administrator. If a node is missing or incompatible, choose a valid link. Do not broaden to global merely to remove an error.

en.title: Audit: find actions and check recording health
en.summary: Use appropriate filters, read outcomes and distinguish an empty list from persistence failure.

sections.heading: What Audit answers
sections.body: Open Audit in the system. Access requires SystemAdmin in the authorized Runtime. Audit records protected actions and outcomes: who attempted which operation on which resource and when. Administrative success does not prove a pump physically started; inspect command feedback and TAGs. Audit does not replace alarm.events, operational.events or Historian readings. This screen queries/diagnoses and does not edit occurrences.

sections.heading: Query fields
sections.body: Leave optional filters empty to broaden the query. Filled filters combine: a record must satisfy all of them. Values are exact, not free-text fragments. Copy values from a known event instead of guessing IDs. Editing filters does not query until Query is selected.

fields.label: From
fields.description: Start in browser local time, converted to UTC for querying. Empty means no lower time bound.
fields.constraints: Must not be later than To.

fields.label: To
fields.description: End of period; the entered instant is included. If an event is missing, check timezone and period before assuming loss.

fields.label: User / subject
fields.description: Stable actor identity recorded in the event, not necessarily display name or login. Copy it from event details.

fields.label: Action
fields.description: Exact recorded operation name. Start with period/outcome if you do not know it.

fields.label: Outcome
fields.description: All leaves outcome unrestricted. Succeeded means recorded as successful; Denied is an authorization rejection; Failed is an unsuccessful operation.

fields.label: Resource kind (advanced)
fields.description: Target category, not the action name or TAG type.

fields.label: Resource / key (advanced)
fields.description: Exact target identifier used by the event. May be a key/path or ID depending on the operation; it is not always a UUID.

fields.label: Area (advanced)
fields.description: Area recorded in action context. A filter does not add an area to an event lacking one.

fields.label: Correlation ID (advanced)
fields.description: Links records from the same request/flow when correlation is provided. Not the individual event ID.

fields.label: Events per page
fields.description: Limits records shown on each page. Changes neither retention nor total stored records.
fields.constraints: Integer from 1 to 1000.

sections.heading: Procedure: investigate a denial
